(6) Humans Tolerate, Machines Cannot

Human Interpretation:

  • Vague descriptions
  • Inconsistent naming
  • Wrong servers
  • Missing authentication info
  • Missing examples

(8) Findings from 6000+ Public APIs

  • Broken specs:
    • Invalid or unparsable OpenAPI Docs
    • Missing path parameters / broken `$ref` chains
    • Invalid examples
  • Poor consumer experience:
    • Examples missing
    • Inconsistent naming, unclear HTTP verb usage
    • Vague or generic descriptions
  • Security runtime challenges:
    • No servers or wrong envs
    • Auth info missing (outside OpenAPI)
    • Stale / outdated OpenAPI Documents


Are APIs AI-Ready? Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(9) Typical Ambiguity Example

  • It might create an offer
  • It mightreplace an user
  • It mightpartially update a offer
  • It mightpatch only some offer fields

(11) The Rise of DX

  • 2000s: Having any API is good
  • 2010s: Having many APIs is good
  • 2020s: Having good APIs is good


From Developer Experience (DX) to Agent Experience (AX) Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(12) API Developers

  • A lot of API-related experience and context
  • Discovering APIs at design time for writing applications
  • Navigating the API landscape with all their human skills


From Developer Experience (DX) to Agent Experience (AX) Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(13) Developer Superpowers

  • Developers resolve naming inconsistencies
  • Developers search, guess, test, troubleshoot
  • Developers understand business workflows through experience
  • Developers catch many mistakes the API design team made


From Developer Experience (DX) to Agent Experience (AX) Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(14) Do Your DX Homework

  • Most API descriptions need quality improvements anyway
  • Better descriptions benefit everyone, not just AI agents
    • Complete and meaningful operation summaries
    • Comprehensive examples for all operations
    • Clear error handling
    • Consistent terminology and naming
  • Good DX is the foundation for good AX


From Developer Experience (DX) to Agent Experience (AX) Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(15) Agentic API Users

  • Little knowledge of API patterns and practices
  • Discovering APIs at run-time for solving tasks
  • Navigating only machine-readable parts of the API landscape


From Developer Experience (DX) to Agent Experience (AX) Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(16) Now There's AX Homework, Too

  • AI agents need information developers don't typically require:
    • Everything that developers usually just know
    • Treat every API like an external one for developers with no context
  • OpenAPI Initiative (OAI) might add AX-specific fields
  • Until then, leverage description fields strategically


From Developer Experience (DX) to Agent Experience (AX) Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(17) The OpenAPI Initiative (OAI)

  • Today: no AX-specific fields in OpenAPI (3.2)
  • Community needs to define what AI agents need (3.3)
  • Tooling will follow once fields are standardized
  • Interested? Join the discussion in the OpenAPI Initiative [https://openapis.org]!

(19) Where to start?



Making APIs AI-Ready Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(20) Readable Summaries and Descriptions

Improves:

  • AI Discoverability, Semantic Clarity, Agent Usability

Where...

  • Objects allowing `summary`: Info, Path Item, Operation, Response, Example, Tag, Reference, ...
  • Objects allowing `description`: Info, Server, Server Variable, Operation, Path Item, External Documentation, Parameter, Request Body, Response, Example, Link, Header, Tag, Reference, Security Scheme, All JSON Schemas, ...


Making APIs AI-Ready Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(21) Semantically Rich Schemas

Improves:

  • AI-Readiness, Agent Usability, Security & Validation

Where...

  • Core JSON Schema fields: type, format, enum, const, required, items, properties, additionalProperties, oneOf, anyOf, allOf, not
  • Constraint fields: minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, minLength, maxLength, pattern, minItems, maxItems, uniqueItems, minProperties, maxProperties
  • OpenAPI locations: components.schemas, inline parameter schemas, request body schemas, response bodies, header schemas, and any reusable schema fragments.


Making APIs AI-Ready Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(22) Correct HTTP Methods

Improves:

  • Agent Usability, Safety, Idempotency Guarantees

Where...

  • Operation verbs: map semantics to methods correctly: GET = retrieve/list, POST = create/trigger, PUT = full replace, PATCH = partial update, DELETE = remove/revoke.
  • Anti-patterns to avoid: state-changing GET, "action verbs" in paths that conflict with methods (for example POST /users/{id}/update).
  • OpenAPI locations: each HTTP method under paths.<path>.<method>, plus consistent naming in operationId, summary and path templates.


Making APIs AI-Ready Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(23) Full Use of "Examples"

Improves:

  • Developer Experience, AI-Readiness, Agent Planning

Where...

  • Single example fields: example on Parameter, Header, Media Type, Request Body, Response, and JSON Schema objects.
  • Multiple examples: examples on Parameter, Header, Media Type, and Link to illustrate variations, error cases, and edge conditions.
  • OpenAPI locations: paths.<path>.<method>.parameters[].example(s), requestBody.content[*].example(s), responses[status].content[*].example(s), components.schemas.*.example.


Making APIs AI-Ready Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(24) Use RFC 9457 Problem Details for Errors

Improves:

  • Error Consistency, Security Signalling, AI Error Reasoning

Where...

  • Standard error schema: define a reusable ProblemDetails in components.schemas following RFC 9457 (for example type, title, status, detail, instance, plus extension members).
  • Error responses: reference the shared schema from responses[4xx/5xx].content['application/problem+json'].schema and optionally the default response.
  • AI benefit: predictable error shapes make it easier for agents to detect, classify, and recover from failures programmatically.


Making APIs AI-Ready Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(25) Appropriate HTTP Status Code Usage

Improves:

  • Foundational Compliance, Agent Usability, Observability

Where...

  • Success responses: use correct 2xx codes: 200 for successful retrieval, 201 for created resources, 202 for accepted/async, 204 for no-content updates or deletes.
  • Error responses: model common 4xx/5xx codes with schemas: 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 500, ... not just a single generic 200 or 500.
  • OpenAPI locations: paths.<path>.<method>.responses[status] with appropriate content, schema and examples per status code.

(28) Jentic's API AI-Readiness Framework

An open source framework which evaluates APIs across six developer & AI-readiness dimensions

  • Foundational Compliance
  • Developer Experience (including tooling compatibility)
  • Agent Experience
  • Agent Usability
  • Security
  • AI Discoverability


Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(29) AI-Readiness Scorecard



Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(30) Foundational Compliance

Evaluates if an API is structurally valid, standards-compliance, and parseable by tooling.

The following signals comprise the dimension:

Signal Description Normalisation
Spec Validity Checks whether the API parses as a valid OpenAPI binary
Resolution Completeness What proportion of $ref references successfully resolve coverage
Lint Results Aggregated quality score from linter diagnostics, weighted by severity inverse weighted categorical
Structural Integrity Measures whether the API's underlying data model is coherent enough for automated reasoning (semantic or logical defects that impact reliable interpretation) logarithmic dampening


Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(31) Structural Integrity Signal



Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(32) Foundational Compliance



Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(33) Developer Experience

Assesses clarity, documentation quality, example coverage, and compatibility with developer tooling.

The following signals comprise the dimension:

Signal Description Normalisation
Example Density Measures coverage of examples across all eligible specification locations coverage
Example Validity Checks all examples for Schema Conformance (JSON + XML) coverage
Doc Clarity Quantifies linguistic clarity of summaries and descriptions. Basically, how easy is it to understand the intent, and the complexity of verbiage. min-max inverted
Response Coverage Presence of meaningful success and error responses across full surface area coverage


Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(34) AI-Readiness & Agent Experience

Evaluates where an API gives enough context for AI systems to understand its intent, constraints, and expected behaviours.

The following signals comprise the dimension:

Signal Description Normalisation
Summary Coverage Measures presence of concise summaries across eligible locations coverage
Description Coverage Measures presence of concise descriptions across eligible locations coverage
Type Specificity Rewards APIs that model values semantically, not just as loosely typed strings weighted categorical
Error Standardisation Favour structured error formats (RFC 9457/7807) coverage
Operation Identifier Quality Evaluate presence and distinctiveness of operationId values composite
Policy Presence Promote inclusion of SLA/rate-limit/policy metadata coverage
AI Semantic Surface Bonus uplift for AI-oriented metadata coverage


Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(35) Agent Usability

Assesses how efficiently agents can navigate, combine, and execute API operations. Measures orchestration safety and agent ergonomics.

The following signals comprise the dimension:

Signal Description Normalisation
Complexity Comfort Measures document size, endpoint density, and schema complexity, penalised using a logistic curve logistic shaping
Distinctiveness Quantifies semantic separation between operations inverse semantic similarity
Navigation (pagination, hypermedia) Evaluates pagination and hypermedia affordances (HATEOAS, JSON:API, HAL) composite
Intent Legibility Evaluates verb-object semantic clarity similarity (LLM assisted)
Safety Evaluates idempotency & sensitive operation protection heuristic penalty
Tool Calling Alignment Represents alignment with LLM tool-calling expectations coverage


Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(36) Security

Assesses if your API protects data, enforces access controls, and follows secure-by-design practices.

The following signals comprise the dimension:

Signal Description Normalisation
Auth Coverage Evaluates whether authentication is correctly applied to sensitive or modifying operations, using intent-aware heuristics heuristic penalty
Auth Strength Auth Strength Measures robustness and correctness of authentication mechanisms declared by the API using normative scores based on IANA auth-schemes, OAuth2, OIDC, API Key placement, and mutual TLS weighted categorical
Transport Security Requires HTTPS for externally exposed hosts binary
Secret Hygiene Detect and penalise hardcoded credentials binary
Sensitive Handling Evaluates the protection of PII/sensitive fields coverage
OWASP Posture Reflect severity-weighted risk findings severity weighted


Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(37) Auth Strength Signal



Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(38) AI Discoverability

Evaluates how easily AI systems can locate, classify, and route to the API across registries, workflows, and knowledge bases.

The following signals comprise the dimension:

Signal Description Normalisation
Descriptive Richness Evaluates the semantic value of textual descriptions within an API description. coverage
Intent Phrasing Evaluates verb-object clarity of summaries and descriptions (Similar to Intent_legibility) semantic similarity (LLM assisted)
Workflow Context Evaluates indicators to workflow specifics including Arazzo/MCP/workflow references. Also analyses existence of callbacks etc. coverage
Registry Signals Detects metadata related to API gateways, llms.txt, APIs.json, MCP registries, externalDocs links to Dev portals. coverage
Domain Tagging Detect domain/taxonomy classification through the use of tags coverage


Measuring what matters Frank Kilcommins: Module 5: Designing AI-Ready API Ecosystems

(39) The Impact of AI Readiness (ROI)

  • 59% ➔ 94% agent retrieval accuracy
  • ~80% model cost reduction
  • ~57% of APIs don't specify both summary & descriptions
